newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares edge up following Wall Street rise.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares edge up following Wall Street rise.

text.p: Russian shares, tracking gains on international markets, advanced further on Tuesday but ended off midsession record levels, after news tax problems could push one big oil producer into bankruptcy and force another to issue shares.
But dealers said they expected the rise to continue.
The Russian Trading System index of 22 shares closed up 0.05 percent to 369.17 on $45.71 million in total market volume.
The index was off its midday record of 369.81, but traders forecast a further rise both in leading shares and second-tier paper. Not all leading stocks have yet hit record levels.
"Cash inflows are now going into Russia," said Regent European Securities Vice-President Dmitry Starenko.
He said investor interest had shifted from second-tier shares into more liquid leading stocks, although demand for the less liquid shares was still high.
"I am not sure we shall reach historical maximums, but the rise will continue," he said.

Nizhnevartovskneftegaz fell to $8.55, off earlier lows, from Monday's closing $10.00, after the government said it would not allow it to restructure its tax debt but would initiate bankruptcy proceedings.
The government also announced it was holding an investment tender for 40 percent of Tyumenskaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya, which owns a controlling stake in Nizhnevartovskneftegaz.

Noyabrskneftegaz NYGS.RTS fell to $10.90 from $11.00 on Friday, when it last traded. The government said it would allow the company, which recently approved a massive increase in authorised but unissued capital, to sell shares to pay off its tax debt.
Among second-tier paper the gainers of the day were Elektrosvyaz telecoms company from Rostov region, which rose to $2.85 from $2.35 at Monday's close and Artelekom which was up to $0.88 from $0.57.

Traders said remaining unsatisfied demand for less liquid shares would spur a price rise in the next few days. They also said the shortage of second-tier paper was increased by regional operators, who sold shares unwillingly.
"People in the regions hold to their packages tightly, they do not see any sense in selling under such a price rise," said IK Prospekt corporate securities director Andrei Ippolitov.
LUKoil ordinaries rose to $16.25 from $15.96 at Monday's close, power utility Mosenergo ordinaries was $1.300 after $1.268.
